title: Compare and order mixed numbers, improper fractions and whole numbers with benchmarks or common denominators

lesson.title: Which One Is Bigger? Lining Up Fractions

steps.say: You already know how to turn a mixed number into an improper fraction, and how to make two fractions have the same bottom number. Today we use those skills for one job: putting mixed numbers, improper fractions and whole numbers in order from smallest to biggest.

Here is the trick. Every fraction, every mixed number and every whole number has a home on the number line. The one further to the right is always the bigger one. So instead of guessing, we just find each number's spot.

visual.caption: Seven quarters sits at one point seven five, two and one quarter sits further right

steps.say: Let's do a real one. Imagine three pieces of ribbon in a Vancouver craft shop. One is two and one quarter metres, one is seven quarters of a metre, and one is three metres. To compare them fairly, we give them all the same bottom number, quarters. Two and one quarter metres is nine quarters. Three metres is twelve quarters. Seven quarters is already in quarters.

visual.caption: Same size pieces means we can just count them

steps.say: Now every number is counted in the same size piece, so we just compare the top numbers. Seven, then nine, then twelve. That means seven quarters is smallest, then two and one quarter, then three. On the number line they go left to right in exactly that order.

visual.caption: From seven quarters all the way right to three

steps.say: Now the mistake I see a lot. Some kids look at one eighth and one quarter and say one eighth is bigger, because eight is bigger than four. But think about a pizza. Cutting it into eight slices gives you smaller slices than cutting it into four. So one eighth is actually the smaller piece. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces, not a bigger fraction.

visual.caption: One slice out of eight is smaller than one slice out of four

steps.say: So whenever you compare, change everything into the same size pieces first, then read them left to right on the number line.

lesson.answer: Same size pieces first, then the number further right on the number line is bigger.

practice.question: At a Kelowna farmers market, Maya buys three bags of apples. The first weighs one and one half kilograms, the second weighs five halves of a kilogram, and the third weighs two kilograms. Draw a number line from zero to three, mark all three weights on it, and write the bags in order from lightest to heaviest.
practice.answer: Change them all into halves: one and one half is three halves, two is four halves, and five halves stays five halves. Since three halves is less than four halves is less than five halves, the order from lightest to heaviest is one and one half kilograms, then two kilograms, then five halves of a kilogram.
